item.title: C/C++ Runtime Methods to Determine System Endianness: Union vs. Pointer Casting
item.description:
“C/C++ Runtime Methods to Determine System Endianness: Union vs. Pointer Casting”

What are the established and portable ways to dynamically check if a system is running in Big-Endian or Little-Endian format, and what are the pitfalls associated with type punning versus using newer language features?

Runtime Endianness Detection Techniques

Several approaches can be employed, each carrying different levels of portability, clarity, and susceptibility to compiler optimization.

1. Using C99 Unions for Type Punning (Generally Accepted)

A classic, well-established method utilizes a union to inspect the memory layout of a multi-byte integer. When an integer is written to the union and then read out byte-by-byte, the order reveals the endianness. This is often preferred over raw pointer casts as it aligns better with C99 standards for initialization (though reading from a non-written union member is technically UB in older standards, initializing the union via a member and reading another is often seen as correct for this specific check). If the first byte of the value 0x01020304 is 1, the system is Big-Endian; if it’s 4, it’s Little-Endian.

This differs fundamentally from the Current Working Directory (CWD), which is where the process was launched from. Since neither the C nor C++ standards inherently define file system concepts like directories, solutions are inherently platform-dependent or rely on library extensions.

The standard approach leveraged here utilizes Python’s built-in signal module, specifically signal.SIGALRM. This method is constrained to UNIX-like operating systems and requires the timeout duration to be an integer value (meaning sub-second precision is not natively supported via this exact mechanism).

Solution Set 1: Applying Time Limits via a Decorator

item.title: Non-Blocking Keyboard Input Detection in C/C++: Exploring Unix and Cross-Platform Techniques
item.description:
“Non-Blocking Keyboard Input Detection in C/C++: Exploring Unix and Cross-Platform Techniques”

Detecting user input instantly without blocking the main application thread is a common requirement in interactive console programs. Since standard input functions (like getchar() or read()) are typically blocking, several specialized techniques must be employed, often differing between operating systems.

Techniques for Non-Blocking Standard Input Monitoring

1. Utilizing select() on Standard Input (File Descriptor 0)

The select() system call allows a program to monitor multiple file descriptors (including standard input, which is descriptor 0) to see if they are ready for reading. This provides a non-blocking way to check for data availability.
